summary: Source-anchored research for MongoDB Major-Version Upgrade Regression Detection. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: Treat published benchmark deltas as workload-scoped until workload and configuration are documented: a systematic review of DBMS comparisons found that tests often did not reflect real-world use cases and reports often lacked enough detail for replication. Percona's upgrade guide recommends testing in a staging environment that closely mimics production, reviewing the current version, hardware, MongoDB usage, and custom settings, and, as part of rollback planning, documenting the deployment's existing state. (medium confidence)

For Atlas Core major-version upgrades, MongoDB recommends validating the target release on staging before production: refresh staging with production data, configure it to resemble production, run application performance and operational tests, and test failover because the upgrade requires a replica set election. A smaller staging tier can make performance tests unrepresentative. (high confidence)

MongoDB 5.0 changed the default global write concern from w:1 to w:majority for replica sets and sharded clusters. A replica-set deployment with at least one arbiter keeps implicit w:1 when its number of data-bearing voting members is not greater than the voting majority; in other scenarios, the default is w:majority. Set an explicit matching write concern when comparing pre-5.0 and later versions: Percona's single-member 4.4-to-7.0 insert test slowed sharply with the 7.0 default, then improved sharply after the test set global write concern back to w:1. A default-behavior change can therefore look like an engine-only regression. (high confidence)

MongoDB's published 8.0 performance process pairs industry benchmarks such as YCSB, Linkbench, TPCC, and TPCH across varied configurations with custom benchmarks based on customer workloads; Percona's upgrade guide also advises testing application-specific queries in a production-like environment. (medium confidence)

Inference from Percona's write benchmark and Sorint's YCSB study: to attribute a performance difference to a server release, hold the workload phase, dataset size, replica-set topology, concurrency, write concern, and WiredTiger cache size constant, or vary them explicitly and report the settings. Sorint's version comparisons differ across workload phases, replica-set architectures, write-concern settings, and cache sizes; its analysis uses 15M records/operations and 128 or 256 threads. Percona's 4.4-to-7.0 example is a single-member, serial one-million-document insert test. These sources do not show how dataset size or concurrency changes version comparisons. (high confidence)

Treat release-performance headlines as workload-specific targets, not expected application uplift. MongoDB's 8.0 upgrade guidance says improvements vary with workload and database configuration; MongoDB's release-team description combines standard benchmark suites with customer workload tests; Percona's independent mongo-perf comparison tests several operation types and thread counts and reports results that vary by concurrency. Run the application's workload before drawing a release-level conclusion. (high confidence)

Compare post-upgrade query response time, throughput, and resource utilization with the pre-upgrade environment; Percona recommends these measures, while Atlas requires performance and operational testing on the staging cluster. (medium confidence)

A version comparison can be confounded by changed write-concern defaults. In one Percona single-member replica-set test, a serial million-insert run took 4 minutes 40 seconds on Percona Server for MongoDB 4.4.18 and 127 minutes on 7.0.11 with defaults; setting 7.0's default write concern to w:1 reduced that run to 10 minutes 26 seconds. This example shows that write concern explains much of this particular gap, but it does not establish a general version effect or eliminate the remaining difference. (low confidence) (verified as of 2024-09-09)
